questions.enonce_markdown:
Given the statements

$p$ : John is sick,

$q$ : John will go to school,

translate into ordinary English the statements

(a) $\sim p \wedge q$,

(b) $\sim(p \wedge \sim q)$. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Read $\sim$ as "not" and $\wedge$ as "and". Negation applies only to the symbol immediately after it (to the whole bracket in (b)).

**(a)** $\sim p \wedge q$ is "(not $p$) and $q$":
$$\boxed{\text{John is not sick and John will go to school.}}$$

**(b)** $p \wedge \sim q$ is "John is sick and John will not go to school", so $\sim(p \wedge \sim q)$ is its negation:
$$\boxed{\text{It is not true that John is sick and will not go to school.}}$$
By De Morgan's law, $\sim(p \wedge \sim q) \equiv \sim p \vee q$, so (b) can also be said as "John is not sick or John will go to school" (equivalently, "If John is sick, then he will go to school").

questions.enonce_markdown:
A relation $R$ is defined on the set of ordered pairs of real numbers by $(a, b)\,R\,(c, d)$ if and only if $a^2 + b^2 = c^2 + d^2$.

Prove that $R$ is an equivalence relation. (7 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
A relation is an equivalence relation if it is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. Work on the set $S = \mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}$ of ordered pairs of real numbers.

**Reflexive.** For any $(a, b) \in S$: $a^2 + b^2 = a^2 + b^2$, so $(a, b)\,R\,(a, b)$.

**Symmetric.** Suppose $(a, b)\,R\,(c, d)$, i.e. $a^2 + b^2 = c^2 + d^2$. Equality of real numbers is symmetric, so $c^2 + d^2 = a^2 + b^2$, that is $(c, d)\,R\,(a, b)$.

**Transitive.** Suppose $(a, b)\,R\,(c, d)$ and $(c, d)\,R\,(e, f)$. Then $a^2 + b^2 = c^2 + d^2$ and $c^2 + d^2 = e^2 + f^2$, hence $a^2 + b^2 = e^2 + f^2$, i.e. $(a, b)\,R\,(e, f)$.

Since $R$ is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, **$R$ is an equivalence relation**. $\blacksquare$

**Geometric meaning.** $(a, b)\,R\,(c, d)$ exactly when the points $(a, b)$ and $(c, d)$ are at the same distance from the origin. The equivalence classes are therefore the circles $x^2 + y^2 = r^2$ centred at the origin ($r \ge 0$; the class for $r = 0$ is the single point $(0, 0)$), and they partition the plane.
